rationale: This sample is a dense floating-point compute kernel suite (flops/fbench/whetstone/pi) with only three tiny functions and 388 bytes of text, so virtually all execution time sits in hot FP loops where control-flow and call-dispatch overhead is maximally damaging; therefore BCF, ICALL, and FLA carry high RuntimeCost/SizeCost weights to suppress their use on hot code, and IGV is down-weighted for both its load-chain overhead on scalar-heavy FP code and its semantic risk around floating-point global state. SUB and SPLIT are favored (low cost weights, high SecurityGain/DiversityGain) because instruction substitution and basic-block splitting add static-only obfuscation value with negligible steady-state runtime impact, while IBR sits in the middle as an acceptable per-block cost for a small binary where a modest code-size increase from branch indirection is tolerable. CorrectnessRisk weights are kept low overall for SUB/SPLIT (well-understood, semantics-preserving transforms) and elevated for IGV and BCF, since altering global-variable resolution or inserting opaque predicates into tight FP loops risks both miscompilation-adjacent behavior and measurable benchmark slowdowns.
